speechtext: Apparel.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
It is also true of most of the apparel industry, which is quite opposed to the approach which the Government has taken in the negotiations over free trade as they affect apparel.
I suggest to the Minister, who is throwing out interjections, that he should spend some talking to the apparel industry. Some of them are small businesses, I say to the Minister. That is what that Minister is responsible for. It is not just the typical manufacturing industries with which Government should be concerned. It is also industries which are less traditional, like tourism. The tourist industry has essentially been abandoned by this Government. There are various ERDA agreements which funnel assistance through the provinces. But the tourist industry is no longer even eligible for help from this Ministry with respect to the kinds of grants and assistance which the Ministry provides to other parts of the economy.
Finally, in looking at some of these sectors, I note the machinery sector of our economy. Surely, by this point we have to realize that you cannot be a sophisticated high technology industrial country without giving real support, real help in the development of a machinery sector. The machinery firms in my constituency tell me absolutely bluntly that what they get from this Government is nothing but hassle. They get harassment in terms of tariff decisions, which I have to spend a good deal of my time trying to straighten out. They get harassment in terms of taxation problems, which also end up in my constituency office. If we did not have at least a few people on this side of the House who are concerned about this sector of our country's economy, so basic to building up a future for us in Canada, the machinery sector would be in much worse shape than it is at this stage.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Nonsense!

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
What do we aim at as a Party in the face of this kind of consistent pattern of failure on the part of the Government in trying to carry its sectorial policies forward? For ourselves, we see the necessity of a highly competitive, high-tech entreprenurial basis to much of our economy so that it can compete internationally. There is no disagreement with respect to that, despite the attempts of the Government to suggest that somehow the New Democratic Party is representative of 20th Century Luddites. But we have a commitment which this Government has not demonstrated to that kind of high-tech part of Canada's economy.
April 20, 1989

Industry, Science and Technology
Secondly, we have a commitment to seeing to it that the the raw material resources of this country are used fully within Canada, instead of being made inputs to the United States manufacturing machine. We want to see the jobs from processing here in this country. We want to see a potential for zinc, which is dug out of the ground in northern Ontario or in the Yukon, to be used in zinc alloy production in Canada. We want to see copper used as an input to copper wire production, heavy electrical cables, in this country, not outside of this country so that the jobs disappear along with the resources. We also want to see that the basic building blocks of a solid industrial core are developed within Canada.
I mentioned the machinery industry as one of these basic building blocks. The chemical sector is another sector that deserves to have much more attention paid to it than has been the case on the part of the Government. If we take these basic building blocks and develop them, out of that will come the type of full employment which is so crucial to our country's future. As the previous speaker has noted, we have perhaps the world's worst industrial adjustment system, with respect to adjustment compensation to workers who are hit by trade changes which this Government has put into effect. Compensation simply does not exist.
We also had very little in the way of adjustment planning to respond to the threats of free trade. All we have to do is look to Europe where we can see that there are all kinds of creative, exciting and workable industrial adjustment interventions that our Government could be taking but is refusing to take. Instead, it is leaving things very much to the mercy of the market.
On our part, we also believe there have to be rules concerning plant shut-downs. It is unforgivable that an American company should decide to transfer production from its Canadian subsidiary in Toronto to its American subsidiary as a consequence of free trade and be able to get away with it scot-free. That is what has happened in the case of Inglis. That is what is happening in the case of Gillette. It is what is happening in the case of Northern Telecom. It should not be possible in a humane country, a country which has labour laws that make sense.

I want to tell this Government that we must change the rules dealing with the problem of plant shut-downs throughout the country.
It is also very important, Mr. Speaker, that we, in Canada, have control over our own economy.

In case after case, the Government has decided simply to let slip absolutely crucial surrenders of control in key parts of the Canadian economy. Mitel is now controlled by a British firm, despite a tremendous amount of government money having gone into the establishment of it. I have talked about Stone Containers and its takeover of Consolidated Bathurst. The loss of Connaught Labs, a part of this country's technological history, a part of our employment future, is something which is unforgivable.
The fact is that Investment Canada, for which the Minister is responsible, has operated simply as a rubber stamp with respect to takeovers. As I view these various takeovers, there has not been a single one rejected during the period of Investment Canada's existence. How can one take seriously an investment review system that has not found it necessary to review even one of thousands of takeovers and say: "That one does not make sense for Canada."? What we have here is in fact a rubber stamp.
We also must have serious support for small business. I direct these remarks directly to the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Hockin) who is now in a position to take some serious steps in this ministry, see to it that it does actually operate to help small-scale firms in the country. The member of our Party who is responsible for small business will be talking about the subject in more detail. However, I hope the Minister will take this task seriously. What I see in my constituency, which is full of small businesses, is that Government does not provide the type of help and support to them which is essential.
We also have to see creative reviews of public enterprise in Canada. There is a pathological rejection on the part of the Government of anything that smacks of socialism despite the fact that in country after country we find effective, profitable and humane public enterprises that are doing an excellent job for people. We in Canada have a long tradition of building such enterprises, mostly at the provincial level, because the federal level has not been prepared to do much except act as a band-aid merchant. The reality is that there is a potential there and I hope the Government recognizes it.

April 20, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
Perhaps the most important point to stress is that any industrial policy which is going to make sense for Canada has to be one which stresses regional fairness. Personally, I must talk about my visit to Cape Breton Island where I saw the tremendous differences in opportunities that exist for people in Cape Breton as compared with those for people in Ontario. It is simply not right. It should not be possible in a country like ours to have this kind of disparity going on generation after generation, so that there are people in Cape Breton who survive perhaps six or eight to a family on the single old age pension cheque of one member of the family who is old enough to receive that pension. It is not right.
It is not right either that on Vancouver Island we have rates of unemployment that are at the immense levels they are in parts of the island. The damage which has resulted from the lack of a serious strategy in the forestry sector is evident on Vancouver Island. The Government has to respond to that.
I could also speak personally about canvassing in Edmonton, the Acting Speaker's home area, and finding people as I went from door to door who had been out of work for months because of the collapse of job opportunities in that city. I could also talk personally about the tremendous disparity that one finds even in the richest part of Newfoundland, in St. John's itself. The difference between life in St. John's for a person graduating or leaving high school and the opportunities that are available to the same person in the City of Toronto are differences which simply should not exist in a humanitarian and fair country.

I can say the same thing about the Province of Quebec where, in many communities, the unemployment rate is so high that young people cannot find jobs. That situation is just as unacceptable in the rest of the country. We cannot have a united country if young men and women are discriminated against and if people living in Quebec do not enjoy the same opportunities as residents of Ontario. It is unfair!
I think the worst thing about this Bill, and the reason we will be opposing it, is that this Bill is part of an ongoing attack with respect to regional development in this country. We already have a freeze with respect to renegotiation of economic and regional development agreements with the provinces throughout this country. Seven provinces and two territories are affected. There are 44 sub-agreements to a total of $918.3 million which has lost its reality as of March 31 and which this Government is not carrying forward to renegotiation at this stage.
We also have stories now circulating with comments coming from the officials within the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, as it still is, saying that there will be more cuts and that these cuts are going to affect the hard-hit regions of this country, regions that were promised prosperity, thanks to free trade. They are now being given the reality of cut-backs, more unemployment, more broken promises as a consequence of what has taken place on the part of the Government. But most of all what we have in this Bill is one more step with respect to the dismantling of any over-all responsibility in this country for regional development. In that sense, this Bill is one more backward step for regional fairness in Canada.
All of this breaks the promise that was made last October in Saint John by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who said, "The federal Government has a responsibility for regional development in the interest of national unity as well as in the interest of fairness. We cannot have two Canadas in the economic sense any more than in the constitutional sense".
This Department used to be responsible for all co-ordination. That is destroyed by this Bill. It is not part of this Bill. We will therefore fight this Bill, and we will do so at this stage by moving an amendment. I move, seconded by the Member for Mission-Coquitlam (Ms. Langan):
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "that" and substituting the following therefor:
"this House declines to give second reading to Bill C-3 because it fails to clearly define federal Government responsibility for regional development and specifically fails to reflect the requirement of s. 36 (l)(b) of the Constitution Act, 1982 that Parliament is committed to ''furthering economic development to reduce disparity in opportunities"."

Mr. Speaker, in 1976, Leonard Peltier, an American Indian, was fraudulently extradited to the United States as a result of a false affidavit submitted by the FBI to A Canadian Court. This fraud was only discovered after Leonard Peltier was returned to the United States and tried in the American courts.
It is totally unacceptable that Canada should tolerate such action from the United States, its neighbour and ally.
This week, the Committee for the Defence of Leonard Peltier is demonstrating on Parliament Hill, asking the Canadian Government to demand the return of Peltier to Canada for a new and fair hearing.
The committee is also making an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada to cancel Peltier's extradition order and have him returned to this country. I ask the Government and the House to pay serious attention to this sad episode in Canada-U.S. relations and to support the corrective action proposed by the Leonard Peltier Defence Committee.

subtopic: ATLANTIC CANADA-CAT .1. FOR CONTINUATION OF FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
ATLANTIC CANADA-CAT .1. FOR CONTINUATION OF FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since 1984 Atlantic Canada has experienced
tremendous economic growth under this Government. Many of the difficulties we experienced in the past have been addressed. I do not want to see this trend diminished in any way.
Our present interest rate policy, which I do not question, is being used to combat inflationary pressures. Inflation, however, is not the problem in Atlantic Canada. Continued growth will be our challenge in the coming years.
To achieve this it is imperative that the economic initiatives and infrastructure programs currently in place for Atlantic Canada be continued and enhanced.
I urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to recognize the fragility of Atlantic Canada in his upcoming Budget and ask him not to impose austerity measures which, coupled with high interest rates, will destroy that which we have achieved in the past four years.

subtopic: EL SALVADOR AND GUATEMALA-HUMAN RIGHTS ABUSES
EL SALVADOR AND GUATEMALA-HUMAN RIGHTS ABUSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of Central America continue to serve on the front lines of the struggle for social justice.
As you may be aware, in El Salvador last night treasury police officers entered an office of an organization involved in refugee settlement and detained approximately 50 peace brigade workers, among them an Australian woman and her three-month old baby.
In Guatemala, the human rights abuses continue. It is into this atmosphere that four members of the RUOG the Guatemalan opposition, have re-entered Guatemala in order to participate in a national dialogue to bring about peace.
I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to make it clear to both Governments the importance that this country places on human rights in that region, in particular to condemn the action of the treasury police in El Salvador, and in Guatemala to give clear assurances that the rights of the four members of the RUOG will be preserved.

April 20, 1989

subtopic: PERFORMANCE OF HURRICANE GROUP OF AMOS
PERFORMANCE OF HURRICANE GROUP OF AMOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Harrica-na group of Amos is taking on the automobile subcontracting market and wants to increase its forestry equipment exports to Latin America and Asia.
The Arcand brothers are also interested in investment opportunities in Chile, which is undertaking a major forestry development program.
Last year, sales of the Harricana group amounted to $41.2 million, up 74 per cent from the previous fiscal year.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians and Quebecers should watch the performance of the Harricana group managers and employees in Abitibi.

Mr. Speaker, last year some Members of the House and the RCMP were made aware of circumstances concerning alleged breaches of trust with respect to House of Commons budgets and funds.
Another Member of the House has now been charged with Criminal Code offences and it is essential that we in this House assure to the accused a fair hearing and that innocence will be presumed until then.
However, every healthy institution, and in particular the institution of this House of Commons, must have the means of assuring its own good order and discipline. Even a local hockey team has the means of applying order and discipline in its organization.
Initiatives to deal with such matters are met by Government statements in sequences such as: "Under police investigation," "sub-judice" and, after the trial, "The matter is closed".
We, the Members who sit in arguably the most powerful institution in this country, are seen by our voters to be totally impotent.
The subcontracting out to provincial courts of serious matters such as these detracts from the strength and honour of the House and its Members.
I respectfully suggest that the burden of such housekeeping lies with the Members here. Whether such business constitutes a matter of privilege or simply doing the work we are paid for and sworn to do, the voters of my constituency and of the country will not want to be stonewalled for another three years.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE EDUCATION FUNDING PROVIDED BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
CO-OPERATIVE EDUCATION FUNDING PROVIDED BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to announce today on behalf of my colleague, the Hon. Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest), the approval of $9 million to advance more than 50 co-operative education projects across Canada. This amount is added to the $26 million that has supported 193 projects since 1985.
Co-operative education is an academic plan that formally integrates a student's classroom studies with work experience in appropriate fields.
The principle of co-operative education was first adopted in Canada in 1957. Since then, co-operative education has grown gradually and spread to both universities and colleges in various regions of Canada.
With the introduction of the Canadian Jobs Strategy funding by Employment and Immigration in 1985, co-operative education has experienced accelerated growth. Today there are 38,000 students enrolled in co-op programs in 75 post-secondary institutions.
Co-operative education will play an important role in the future development and adaptability of our workforce. It is a well suited mechanism to assist young Canadians in preparing themselves for the workplace of tomorrow.
Co-op education serves as a major bridge between the classroom and the world of work. Our Government is committed to programs that ease the school-work transition.
Our support for co-operative education illustrates our Government's commitment to the human resources strategy and the training measures announced on April 11, when the Government brought forth its labour force development strategy.
April 20, 1989

Most important, we see our support of the co-op education movement as an investment in people that will pay valuable dividends in the future.

Mr. Speaker, Canada Post is cutting its ties with the Canadian people and moving silently toward its ultimate goal, the complete privatization of the postal system.
The evidence is clear and overwhelming. Late last week the Post Office in Port Coquitlam, British Columbia, removed the Canadian flag flying over its two postal operations and replaced it with Canada Post's own ugly grey corporate flag. This has been repeated in Winnipeg and Halifax and is spreading across the country.
At the same time Canada Post has adopted a new logo. Look at it. It removes the name "Canada" from the very presentation at the post office. Canada Post, not "Mail/ Poste", must remain a Crown corporation. It must continue to be accountable to the people of Canada. It must continue to provide satisfactory services to all areas of the country, and it must continue to fly the Canadian flag at every location in every community in this wonderful country.

Mr. Speaker, April 16 to 22 is National Citizenship Week. If some people wonder exactly what we are celebrating in National Citizenship Week, it may be because their citizenship seems as natural to them as being born; they became Canadian citizens at birth without even realizing it.
I believe that our fellow citizens who were born in other countries are perhaps in a better position to appreciate what Canadian citizenship really means.
Canada has rightly been called the world's first international country. We owe this reputation to our respect for the various cultures in our society.
5. ft 31
National Citizenship Week no doubt gives us the best possible opportunity to reflect on how lucky we are to be citizens of Canada and to live in one of the most beautiful countries in the world, a land of democracy, peace and freedom.

subtopic: COVERAGE OF ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S EDUCATION FUNDING CAMPAIGN
COVERAGE OF ABORIGINAL PEOPLE'S EDUCATION FUNDING CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has found a powerful ally in its indifferent and insulting treatment of native students and the native community. It is the media.
The media, like the Government, pretends that a new policy to deny natives full access to education is inconsequential, when it should be front page news.
The native community's peaceful but powerful demonstration against this outrage has received little attention.
Post-secondary education is essential for native people to have access to employment, to develop future leaders, to promote independence and self-government. Increased investment in education will reduce welfare costs, imprisonment, and the tragically high rate of native youth suicide.
The Government and the media pretend not to hear the outcry from native people who are fighting for their future.
I call on the Government and the media to recognize the voice of the native community and support the obligation of Government to provide full access to education.

Mr. Speaker, this morning, the Minister for External Relations (Mrs. Landry) commented on the situation in Lebanon. I think the Government should take advantage of the unanimous feeling in the House now that Canada is a member of the United Nations Security Council to take a determined stand and urge the United Nations to put pressure on all warring parties in the Middle East, in order to put an end to the situation in Lebanon and get rid of all

April 20, 1989
foreign troups in that country. I think that Canada now has a good opportunity to take this initiative and that Canadians of Lebanese descent realize that the Canadian Government is concerned about this problem in the Middle East and that it wants the Lebanese to live in safety and peace, in their own homes.

maintopic: OPPOSITION TO EARLY RELEASE OF DANGEROUS OFFENDERS
OPPOSITION TO EARLY RELEASE OF DANGEROUS OFFENDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, each of us in this House has recently read about dangerous criminals who, while on parole, commit violent crimes. These unfortunate and despicable incidents occur all too frequently. These crimes could be avoided if the Canadian parole system regulations were toughened. We must prevent the early release of dangerous offenders who have committed senseless and brutal crimes.
My constituents have expressed their disgust at the persistence of these unnecessary and tragic offences. We must all take responsibility and work toward a system in which dangerous offenders are not allowed to repeat their violence.
I call upon the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) to review immediately and tighten up the regulations so that all Canadians are better protected from violent and dangerous offenders.

Mr. Speaker, there is a lethal epidemic sweeping the Province of Ontario, one that is fast becoming a national tragedy. The epidemic I am referring to is the use of cocaine and a cocaine derivative called crack.
A recent report from the Centre of Forensic Sciences stated that a total of 95 deaths in Ontario last year involved cocaine-nearly five times the 20 deaths recorded in 1985. These figures provide graphic evidence of the increase in human wastage due to drug abuse.
The figures tell another story as well. Many of the recent deaths have been attributed to pure or nearly pure cocaine hitting the drug market.
According to Metro Toronto Drug Squad intelligence, cocaine purity is up and prices are down. A gram of the drug now sells for between $100 and $150, half of what it sold for in 1985.
These figures tell me that we are losing the war against drugs, especially the battle against cocaine. The extent of the problem can best be illustrated by the fact that for the first time in the history of the Metro Toronto Police cocaine busts outnumber arrests for marijuana. So far this year, 824 seizures of cocaine have been made compared to 520 of marijuana.
With the phenomenal rise in cocaine use, can the drug wars be far behind? I urge the Government to step up its campaign against drugs before Toronto becomes Washington North.

Mr. Speaker, years ago when I was going to high school in Thunder Bay, I rode the bus with a number of young native people of my age from the Fort William Indian Reserve. None of those young people made it through to grade 13.
Last fall during the federal election campaign when I had the opportunity to speak to the first of what has become many rallies at the Indian Affairs office in Thunder Bay, I was very, very pleased to see in the crowd not only the children of those people with whom I went to school going to university and college but their parents going back to school as well. That was the result of the old E-12 guidelines that allowed full access by aboriginal peoples to post-secondary education.
I call on the Government to give these people the chance they want and deserve for their future. Suspend the current guidelines, give them a year to negotiate and develop a program that will meet everyone's needs, particularly those of the aboriginal peoples.
April 20, 1989

subtopic: CAMPAIGN TO CLEAN UP HAZARDOUS WASTE SITES
CAMPAIGN TO CLEAN UP HAZARDOUS WASTE SITES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians across Canada are pleased to know that the Government is committed to protecting the environment.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) in this House, along with his provincial counterparts, has established a five-year fund to clean up hazardous waste sites in Canada. Some $250 million will be available to cover the cost of cleaning up sites, the owners of which are not known. In cases where owners can be found, they will be forced to pay the clean-up costs.
I am of course very pleased with this new development in the fight against dangerous material, whether it be on the ground or in the air. Acid rain has been one of my causes throughout my career in the House.
The diplomacy the Minister has demonstrated in getting the provincial Ministers to agree has given me hope that we will soon have more agreements that are honest attempts at solving these very difficult problems.

subtopic: EFFECT OF FREE TRADE AGREEMENT ON FARMERS
EFFECT OF FREE TRADE AGREEMENT ON FARMERS
speechtext:

The food conglomerate H. J. Heinz Company of Canada has said that it will find it necessary to move to the United States. In fact, a person from Nabisco Brands Limited, Ray Verdon, has said that he advised firms to cut costs, for example, by using potential U.S. sources as low-cost suppliers.
I stand today to call on the Deputy Prime Minister to do the right thing, to bring in programs to help farmers who are adversely affected by free trade.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER MEET STUDENTS
REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER MEET STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my last question is for the Right Hon. Prime Minister.
Native students have stated that they want to talk directly with the Prime Minister. Does the Prime Minister agree to talk with the students affected by this program?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER MEET STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that the Minister responsible is handling this issue with great openness and, I trust, generosity to our native people, as he should.
However, his requirements are minimal. He says that his door is wide open. Furthermore, he meets with native leaders on a regular basis. He met with some students and he says that his door is wide open to receive the delegations. On the other hand, he asks that they end their hunger strike. That does not seem too much to ask. And the reason for my optimism, once the strike is over, are the measures that the House has approved in the last four years.
This program that is so important for our future native leaders was increased from $53 million in 1984 to $130 million this year. The number of native students eligible for this program has increased from 8,000 in 1984 to 15,000 this year.
I think that this program was endorsed by all parties here in the House of Commons. It is an indication of our general position in favour of native young people. We want to do more.
And the Minister has shown not only great leadership but also generosity toward the native leaders in order to put an end to this tense situation as soon as possible and to do more in future.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He will know that the report of the Thalidomide Task Force is both a comprehensive and a demonstrative document which outlines the extraordinary needs of some 120 courageous young men and women. The Minister will also know that these individuals face enormous difficulties in education, transportation, career related matters, and in a host of health related issues.
Would the Minister indicate to the House when he will be announcing a compensation package which has been sought for many years by these victims and by those individuals who have ably represented them over the years?
Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and
Welfare): Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question on a very important matter.
I had the opportunity to meet with the members of the Thalidomide Victims Association. I do not think anyone who met with them would be anything but struck by the sincerity of their condition and also the seriousness of it as well.
The Government is currently considering the request that has been made. There have been a number of requests that have been made for extraordinary payments to people who have been damaged in a number of different ways through medications and through other procedures. We are considering those, and when we have an announcement to make we will be making it.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same Minister. I remind him of a quote from a statement which was made by a former Minister in the Diefenbaker Government. On January 29, 1963, the Hon. J. Waldo Monteith said:
It is our job to ensure that thalidomide victims are cared for in the
best possible manner, that their needs are met to the fullest extent
we can devise and to ensure, as much as possible, that a similar
tragedy will never occur again.
April 20, 1989

Oral Questions
I ask the Minister, not on the grounds of legal precedent but on the grounds of a moral obligation on the part of the Government of Canada, will he come forward quickly and announce a compensation package, not in six months, not in nine months, but will he indicate a date of a possible announcement for a compensation package for these survivors?

subsubtopic: LEBANON-PLIGHT OF REFUGEES-CONSULAR SERVICES IN CYPRUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for External Relations. It concerns the deteriorating situation in Lebanon which is producing a flood of very desperate refugees in record numbers.
This morning the Minister announced that a single immigration officer will be sent to Cyprus to facilitate applications to Canada. However, with all due respect, I suggest to the Minister and the Government that that does not come close to meeting the magnitude of the problem.
I ask the Minister, given that people cannot be expected to travel safely to Damascus, Syria, where we have a full consular operation, and given that one immigration official in Cyprus will not come close to meeting the flood of applications that can be expected, will the Minister, at least on a temporary basis, establish a full and proper immigration consular operation that will be capable of meeting the demand, instead of placing one person in an untenable situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
subsubtopic: LEBANON-PLIGHT OF REFUGEES-CONSULAR SERVICES IN CYPRUS
speechtext: Indeed, Mr. Speaker, an External Affairs official was sent to Cyprus. And very special steps have been taken so that no one is sent back from Lebanon until further notice. As my colleague said yesterday, the government put a stop on April 6 to the removal of people to Lebanon. Immigration services are provided and, of course, any organization, any individual can, under the special program, sponsor a Lebanese relative at his or her request. Special steps have therefore been taken. We are closely monitoring the situation and we can give people the assurance that we will take the humanitarian stance for which Canada is well knoun.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS HIGH COMMISSION ON REFUGEES-REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY MEETING
UNITED NATIONS HIGH COMMISSION ON REFUGEES-REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the special program on this side of the ocean where we try to sponsor people from here, but the problem is not in Canada. The problem is on the other side of the world where people cannot make their way to Damascus; and one person in Cyprus, with every respect, does not come close to the reality and the emergency of the situation.
I ask the Minister to reconsider her stand. I further ask the Minister, given that my colleagues earlier this week have asked for leadership by this Government at the United Nations, and given that the United Nations' High Commission on Refugees has only a skeleton staff of three people in Lebanon to deal with the flood of human misery, will the Minister give the House her undertaking that she will ask the UNHCR to convene an emergency meeting in order to try to reinforce this commitment in Lebanon, so that an international commitment can address this human tragedy, and so that other countries will be encouraged to try to land people who are desperate and needy?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)

Mr. Speaker, in addition to the special steps I referred to earlier, mention must be made of our cooperation with the Red Cross and the substantial sums of money that were sent to help the victims of strife in Lebanon. Obviously, such situations are regrettable and the Canadian government will do everything it can.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Communications. Rogers Cable admits its investment in CNCP is the first step toward competing in Canada's long-distance telephone market. Given that most Canadians know that long-distance competition favours big business, not the little guy, will the Minister assure Canadians that his Government supports affordable phone service across the country? Will he reject a national policy of long-distance competition if it raises local rates and cuts a lifeline for a grandmother who cannot afford to pay?

Mr. Speaker, several years ago, the Government announced its policy on that issue which involves universality among other things. Now, if some groups want to get in touch with the CRTC, that Commission has the legal authority to answer the Hon. Member's questions.

Given that this could happen in many parts of the country, which would be a disaster if it did, will the Minister assure Canadians that rather than blind faith in telephone competition his national priority is affordable telephone service for all Canadians?

subsubtopic: CFB GOOSE BAY-LOW-LEVEL FLIGHTS-TREATMENT OF INNU PROTESTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked a question of the Right Hon. Prime Minister having to do with the future of Innu protesters in Labrador. At that time the Prime Minister tried to fob off the question by pretending that this is a matter of provincial jurisdiction and that it is not really something about which he ought to be concerned.
I presume that the Prime Minister will know that since I asked him that question 75 Innu natives who went to the Canadian Armed Forces Base to present a letter peacefully were rounded up by the military police who are employees of the Government of Canada, the federal Government, the Government which the Prime Minister leads.
Is the Prime Minister now prepared to take his responsibility as the Prime Minister of the federal Government and to intervene in this matter to bring an end to the low-level flight testing, to declare the moratorium that people have been asking for, and to reach the negotiated settlement with the Innu that the court judgment of the other day recommends and that many people have been recommending to the Government for many years now?

April 20, 1989
Oral Questions

No arrests were made and no charges were laid.

Order!

Order!

By the Prime Minister.

subsubtopic: QUERY WHEN MINISTER WILL MEET WITH ALBERTAN FRANCOPHONES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State. Last year, Alberta and Saskatchewan passed bills repealing minority language rights in those provinces. We know that Saskatchewan signed a memorandum of understanding with the Federal Government to try and compensate a little for the harm done to its minority by that bill. Alberta Francophones have been trying for
April 20, 1989

some time to meet with the Secretary of State, who is responsible for promoting and protecting minorities. When will the Secretary of State meet with these people to discuss an agreement between Alberta and the Federal Government which would help them survive in their own province?

subtopic: MINORITY LANGUAGE RIGHTS - REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MINORITY LANGUAGE RIGHTS - REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I thank the Minister for that answer. You were going to jump over Alberta going to B.C. Now that you are going to stop over, I am happy to hear that.
I want to ask the Prime Minister a question. We have a serious question in Canada dealing with minority language rights in our provinces. We know that there is a crisis in many provinces at this time. I have asked, and the Liberals have asked, before for a conference of the Premiers of this country to discuss the distressing situation of some minority groups in Canada. I am wondering if the Prime Minister read the Official Languages Report. The Commissioner recommends a Royal Commission, or at least a federal-provincial conference, on that question, to settle once and for all the future of minority rights in this country. Will he accede to that request, not from us, but from the Official Languages Commissioner, and call a federal-provincial conference on that question?

subtopic: MINORITY LANGUAGE RIGHTS - REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend referred to the comments of the Commissioner of Official Languages. Indeed, on April 7, the Commissioner wrote to the Government saying that, "The new Act for which the Government was responsible is eloquent testimony of your Government's commitment to greater linguistic harmony and equality".
Oral Questions
That commitment is of course the position of the Government of Canada, and I know it is the position shared by all Parties in the House of Commons.
There are challenges facing minority language groups across the country which vary from province to province. We have a large French-speaking minority in the Province of Ontario, an English-speaking minority in the Province of Quebec, and so on. I had occasion on April 14, 1988, in the Province of Saskatchewan and in the presence of Premier Devine, to make a comment dealing with precisely this issue. I think it would perhaps answer my hon. friend's question, and I ask for his indulgence to respond in the same way.
Saskatchewan is 97 per cent English speaking. Let us assume that the population were 97 per cent French speaking in Saskatchewan. How would you want them to be treated? What rights would then be fair for the English-speaking minority in Saskatchewan? I suppose that you would want the rights in regard to the courts, the legislature, in regard to schools, all the rights of Canadian citizens.
If you want to understand how you should deal with minorities, ask yourself what it would be like to be in the position of a linguistic minority and treat that minority with all of the generosity that you would want extended to yourself.
That is my position, and that is the position of the Government of Canada, and I believe it to be the position of all Members of this House.

subtopic: MINORITY LANGUAGE RIGHTS - REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. This Government has made much of the benefits of the trade deal entered into between Canada and the United States. Speech, speech.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benoit Tremblay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as part of today's debate on the Bill to establish the Department of Industry, Science and Technology, I welcome this opportunity to draw the attention of the House to the issue of regional economic development and the role the new Department will play in this area.
In 1984, the federal Government realized that despite the very substantial efforts and monies expended on regional development so far, serious regional economic disparities continued to exist throughout the country.
In the fall of 1986, a new, decentralized approach to regional development was announced in the Throne Speech. This approach consists in correcting the imbalances between regions, stressing the most disadvantaged
Industrie, Science and Technology
areas and using the federal Government's scarce resources more effectively. More specifically, and this was a major change, Mr. Speaker, which is reflected in this Bill, programs will be adapted to local circumstances and needs; the regions concerned will be more involved in decision-making; and all local resources will be explored when developing strategies.
On the basis of these principles, new, decentralized initiatives for regional development have been designed, according to the needs of the various regions.
Unlike the formula used previously, the Government's new approach is based on delegation of authority to the regions for the development, co-ordination, and funding of their programs. For the first time, Mr. Speaker, the federal Government has truly established a partnership with the regions. The Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is responsible for regional development in the Atlantic Provinces, the Department of Western Economic Diversification covers the four Western provinces, and Industry, Science and Technology Canada is responsible for regional development in Ontario and Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, each of these three agencies has received a clear mandate for the development of the region for which it is responsible, for co-ordinating its activities and designing and financing programs adapted to regional needs.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill will complete the process of reorganization that is necessary to implement the objectives of regional development in Canada. Industry, Science and Technology Canada is now establishing an organizational structure, separate from the rest of the Department, that will be responsible for regional development in Ontario and Quebec.
In Ontario regional development activities are adapted to the circumstances in the various regions in that province.
Activities include managing current programs for business development, such as FEDNOR, an initiative to promote the development of Northern Ontario; administering the economic and regional development agreement between Ontario and the federal Government; preparing regional development policies and methods for Ontario's subregions; establishing and implementing new programs adapted to the needs of the subregions; and finally, defending the interests of Ontario subregions when national policies and programs are being designed; co-ordinating all federal regional development activities in that province; and monitoring and analysing the development of the economies of the provinces in the subregions.

April 20, 1989
Industrie, Science and Technology
Among all Canadian provinces, Ontario of course has been enjoying the most prosperous economy in recent years, but this has not always been the case. In 1980-81, for example, Ontario lost 31,000 residents to immigration. In 1986 it recorded a positive immigration of 40,000 people. Regional development assistance must be tailored to that reality, and the need for federal help in terms of regional economic development is much less significant. Still, economically speaking Ontario can be divided into three major regions: the industrial core centred around Toronto and the metropolitan area whose growth these past few years has been the fastest among industrialized nations and whose unemployment rate is certainly half that of other Canadian major urban areas; the centre of Ontario, a much more heterogeneous aggregate of rural and urban regions; and, finally, Northern Ontario whose economy is resource-based, where unemployment has been severe for years, and where personal income is relatively much lower than in other communities.
Mr. Speaker, this is why FEDNOR has been set up to meet the needs of Northern Ontario. It enables the region to take part in the preparation and administration of programs and to be party to the decision-making process.
FEDNOR was given a five-year mandate and a budget of $55 million. It provides financing solely for private sector profit-making undertakings, particularly small-and medium-sized businesses. The amount of financial assistance is geared to projected economic fallouts, viability, risks, credibility, and needs.
FEDNOR's mission is to promote the diversification of the local economy, the on-site processing of natural resources, the development and acquisition of new technologies, as well as the higher competitiveness and productivity of businesses.
FEDNOR has a three-pronged program. The Basic Industrial Program is designed to help Northern Ontario's new and long-established concerns involved in manufacturing, processing or aquafarming or offering repair or other services. It supports projects aimed at establishing, expanding or upgrading various facilities, cariying out feasibility studies, as well as corporate innovation and marketing activities.
The Small Rural Business Assistance Program is for new or existing businesses in the rural regions of Northern Ontario. It is open to people dealing in manufacturing and processing, forestry and aquafarming, as well as to such services as retail sales, wholesales, warehousing, repairs and the like. Applications under this program are also accepted for projects related to the establishement, expansion or upgrading of facilities.
And finally the Loan Insurance Program which provides new or existing companies with loan insurance covering up to 85 per cent of loans made by recognized lending institutions for establishing, expanding or upgrading facilities.
Thanks to these programs, companies in Northern Ontario, especially the small and medium-size businesses, are getting the type of financial assistance they need to stimulate local economic activities which will benefit the people in the area.
Based on local participation and under the direction of an advisory committee made up of 12 local representatives, FEDNOR demonstrates the value of the new decentralized approach of the federal Government in the area of regional development, as well as our goal of partnership with the regions.
The Government and ISTC have also taken an entirely new approach to regional development in Quebec.
To be fair and efficient, the new federal programs take into account the fact that Quebec is made up economically of two broad groups of regions whose types and levels of development differ considerably.
In spite of a relatively rapid growth over the past few years, economic disparities between most Quebec regions and Canada as a whole, but especially Ontario, persist, and in some cases are getting worse. That is why the approach to regional development covers the whole province of Quebec.
FIRST of all, there is the industrial sector of Quebec which is based in the Greater Montreal area, and covers most of the Southwestern part of the province. This economic region is very well integrated in the North American economy, but is lagging far behind its competitors in the Southwestern area of Ontario and the Northeastern part of the United States. Moreover, the proportion of jobs provided by traditional industries is much higher than in the other areas I have just mentioned.
April 20, 1989

The second part of the program is aimed at the outlying areas which extend from the East to the North West and whose economy, based on resources, is similar to that of the Atlantic provinces. With the exception of Eastern Quebec, these areas have received no special attention under the previous regional development program.
The comparison with other parts of Canada clearly shows the need for special regional development action in Quebec, both in the natural resources regions and the central regions.
On June 9, 1988, the federal Government and Quebec signed a five year agreement whereby they will invest $440 million and $380 million respectively to promote the economic development of the Quebec regions. Moreover, the federal Government has implemented a $40 million program to help the forest industry in Eastern Quebec. The federal Government and the province have earmarked each $75 million to refinance the auxiliary agreements over the next year. Also, they have just added to these agreements a special program for Montreal East.
The new agreement for the Quebec region development has six major objectives:
- mobilize the local contractors; -encourage the development and processing of natural resources; -promote technological development; -increase the local businesses' competitiveness; -encourage economic diversification; -make it possible for these regions to integrate in the Canadian and North American markets and fully benefit from the Free Trade Agreement between Canada and the United States.
There have been consultations-that is new, Mr. Speaker-to make sure that the people in these areas fully participate in the planning process, and the final text of the agreement takes into account the needs and priorities mentioned by the business people and the authorities in various parts of the province. In each of the regions with a resource base economy, an advisory committee made up of business people and area leaders will ensure the participation of the region in the decision-making process.
The agreement is based on the above principles of decentralization, consultation, and focusing on the areas that are the most in need.
Industrie, Science and Technology
One of the agreement's major goals is to accelerate economic growth in resource-based areas through five components-technological research and development, business enterprise development, resource development, human resources development, and infrastructure strengthening.
First, technological research and development. Since national policies and programs aimed at promoting innovation, technological transfer and research and development cannot always be adjusted to the conditions and needs of small businesses in resource based areas, a program to support research and development has been negotiated. Administered by the various Canadian departments and agencies concerned, will complement any national program in the areas involved without endangering national goals.
The agreement calls for the completion of joint industrial research activities and also joint or supplementary programs for mining and forestry. Further, a federal program for food testing has been announced, and another one involving fisheries and agriculture will be put in place.
Second, business enterprise development. The growth of enterpreneurship and small businesses is the best guarantee for diversification and economic expansion in resource based areas. Programs under that component will supply support similar to that offered in the Atlantic area.
A federal business development program has been established under that element of the agreement. Further, the province will initiate a business diversification and expansion program.
Third, resource development. Resources are the mainstay of regional economies. The activities of departments who deal with national resources often are not enough to solve certain development problems in a given area or to enable it to give its full measure. Programs under that component will be administered by the departments concerned and will endeavour to correct the situation.
Since my time is fast running out, Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize this Government's efforts toward the central areas. The special needs of Quebec's central region also were considered. A federal productivity growth program has been set up. A joint innovation program with the provincial Government is under consideration and the new agreement provides that the province will establish an industrial ajustment program.

April 20, 1989
Industrie, Science and Technology
In addition, special programs for the Montreal area and disadvantaged regions within central Quebec are provided for. We must also recall, Mr. Speaker, the federal Government's special initiative for the sub-region of eastern Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, with these programs, Quebec will finally be able to benefit from the type of regional development assistance that only an effective federal approach, in consultation with the community, can provide.
In conclusion, I wish to say a few words about the Department's regional development activities. If you believe the Opposition Members, the federal Government has reduced its regional development expenditures in Ontario and Quebec with this new approach. Nothing could be further from the truth. In fact, regional development expenditures in Ontario and Quebec have increased considerably since the present Government took office. In the five-year period that preceded our taking power, these expenditures averaged $189 million a year for Quebec and $68 million for Ontario. Over the last five years, from 1984-85 to 1988-89, they rose to $246 million a year for Quebec and $108 million for Ontario.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the Government spent $1,231 million for Quebec and $539 million for Ontario over the last five years, compared to $944 million and $338 million respectively for the previous period.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, the new Department of Industry, Science and Technology gives great importance to regional development in Quebec and Ontario. Work in this area is managed by a separate section of the Department, with qualified personnel in each province and the participation of local councils and communities and even more resources than were allocated to regional development in the past.
Mr. Speaker, if I have a second, I would like to add that the Free Trade Agreement puts the Government under no new constraints as regards business. We have the same rules and obligations as we had and have under GATT.
As well, we have added the ability to solve conflicts much more easily, to reach an understanding under the Agreement before going to court, but also to appeal to the bilateral commission if U.S. legislation threatens to change the rules of the game. That seems to me to be an important gain, both for the whole Canadian economy and for the regional economy.
I would like to add that the regional development responsibility of the Department of Industry, Science and Technology, comparable to that of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and the Western Diversification Department, involves the fundamental role of defending regional interests and, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that this new organization based on partnership with the regions will help us rely more on regional dynamism and ensure the prosperity of Canada's regions.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to enter the debate on Bill C-3, realizing the necessity of launching Canada in new directions. We must understand the implications of the changing global economy and Canada's place in it if the Government is going to play a role in ensuring Canada's continued prosperity.

This Bill goes far beyond the establishment of a department. It gives the government the means to establish the programs and policies which are essential to the well being of Canada.

Within the mandate of this Department are those policies which will determine whether Canada's future is full of hope or despair.

It is essential that Canada recognize the importance of science, engineering and technology if we are to be competitive in foreign markets.

The reality facing Canada today is that we cannot continue merely to rely on the exploitation of our natural resources if we are to maintain our standard of living. In a world in which sustainable development has become a global imperative, in which the continued burning of fossil fuels endangers our health and well-being, we must change our way of thinking, our understanding of economic development in the context of impending environmental crisis.
We have grown up as Canadians believing that our natural resources are unlimited, that our wealth and standard of living is assured. This is simply not true. Our natural resources are limited in supply, and the world demand for them is changing as more and more people consider a clean and healthy environment to be the most important natural resource of all. The question we must now ask ourselves is: Are we prepared to invest in
April 20, 1989

realizing the potential of Canada's most important resource, its people?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The natural wealth we have enjoyed has inhibited an appreciation of the necessity of investing in people, in education and skills, in innovative technologies. All we need to do is to look around us to understand the importance of science, of engineering, and of advanced education, whether it be the common use now of a personal computer, the production of information technologies, or the fusing of two atoms to create energy.
Unfortunately, Canada is being dragged reluctantly into the 21st century. Whether we like it or not, we are engaged in a world-wide race for technological leadership, a race that is being intensified by a number of factors including, for example, international trading competitiveness characterized by the rapid and, in historic terms, relatively easy flow of goods and services between nations, the explosion of information technologies.
Wealth is no longer simply a matter of control of durable goods. Just as brains over brawn has characterized human evolution, so will the innovative use of knowledge prevail over the mining of wealth and the production of goods over the next century. The activities of trans-national corporations, multi-national trading companies and international financial institutions, these corporate entities with the ability to move capital rapidly between nations, limit significantly the ability of nation states to control matters within their own jurisdictions, and involve national governments in major technological enterprises. The United States, through defence procurement, especially in the strategic defence initiative, has created the greatest industrial boondoggle in the history of the world.
In Canada, we have the recent example of the proposed acquisition of Connaught Laboratories by Institut Merieux, a corporation controlled by the Government of France. These factors alone emphasize just how important this Bill really is. Unfortunately, Canada is not well positioned at the present time in the new technologies race.
Industrie, Science and Technology
As Geraldine Kenney-Wallace and Fraser Mustard recently wrote:
Canada's status among developed nations has been largely won by trading grains, fish, metals, lumber, paper, oil, gas and electricity. The domestic manufacturing base, long protected by tariffs that encourage the building of branch plants, grew strong after 1945.
In contrast with other small countries, such as Switzerland, Holland and Sweden, however, Canada has not developed a similar number per capita of world-scale home-based multinational corporations.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), both as candidate and as Leader of the Government, has had a lot to say about science and technology, giving the nation's science community much cause for hope. As candidate for the leadership of his Party, he wrote:
The starting line for me is the technological dimension. Either we go into the game and become important players in this major league, or we become a nation that will, during its entire lifetime, play in the Junior B circuit. Research and development and the resulting innovations, are the lifeblood of a successful economy and country.
The Prime Minister also set an impressive target for levels of performance for research and development at 2.5 per cent of the gross domestic product of Canada, a target he set in 1984. His commentary was accurate and the goal of increasing our level of spending on research and development was achievable. Unfortunately, we also have the Government's record. In November, 1984, $46 million was removed from Environment Canada's budget.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Also in 1984, the Conservative Government announced the elimination of the energy division of the National Research Council. And there are other examples. But still the Government rhetoric was compelling. For example, the Government asked the university research granting councils to submit their five-year plans for their financing needs. In response, the research councils had their base budgets frozen, and inflation eroded them for three more years until a recent announcement of some increase in the base budgets.

April 20, 1989
Industrie, Science and Technology
Everyone who has been following the course of events has warned the Government about the consequences of undermining the research and development effort in Canada. We have had more than our fair share of forums and advisory councils. By way of advisory bodies the Government has assembled eminent Canadians through the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology chaired by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulro-ney). Unfortunately, its proceedings are secret. There has been the Advisory Council on Adjustment, the de Grandpre Commission. We have had for many years the Science Council of Canada. There are many advisory services in the Public Service of Canada. In Ontario, we have recently had the excellent work of the Premier's Council.
In terms of forums the Government has spent a great deal of money and taken people's time on at least two occasions to host the National Forum on Science and Technology and the National Forum on Post-secondary Education. If only some of the recommendations of these organizations and forums were acted upon I am convinced that we would not today be looking at the dismal statistics that I am compelled to cite.
Federal government expenditures on research and development as a percentage of total R and D spending have fallen since 1984 from 37 per cent to 30 per cent in 1988. According to the de Grandpre Commission, Canada has the lowest gross research and development expenditures as a percentage of GDP as compared to eight comparable countries. Industry funded R and D in Canada as a percentage of GDP is the lowest. Government funded research and development in Canada as a percentage of GDP is the second lowest. In terms of government performed R and D as a percentage of GDP, Canada is in the middle. Canada's higher education research and development as a percentage of GDP is the lowest. In terms of domestic patents granted per 100,000 inhabitants, Canada ranks second lowest. In terms of international patents granted, Canada is the lowest. With respect to advanced degrees awarded, Canada is in the middle. Canada has the lowest number of technology intensive industries with positive trade balances. Only 2 per cent of Canadian companies invest in R and D and two-thirds of this R and D is carried out by less than 7 per cent of this group.
The facts drown out the Prime Minister's protestations as to the importance of science and technology. Rhetorically, he has said the right things, but his rhetoric has not been translated into action. All the Government has to offer as a strategy for developing the Canadian economy is megaprojects and market forces. When it comes to building a science culture and an industrial base which is at once innovative and able to interact with the results of fundamental research, this is simply not adequate.
There are also many things for Canadians to be encouraged about. We have in place in Canada an excellent educational system with a population that has historically shown a willingness to support a high priority on education. We have a small but excellent governmental science community. The National Research Council enjoys a proud history of achievement. It is now called upon to evolve, but it must not be abandoned.
We have a vibrant, exciting and eager group of small and medium-sized high tech companies in Canada which have an international outlook, experience in world trade and excellent prospects if they are given the proper support. We have a peaceful, well-educated population by world standards. Given the proper tools and encouragement we can work smarter than anyone else.
With these strengths on our side, I ask myself where this Government is taking us, driven as it is by a preoccupation with deficits. Our existing significant investment in universities is being allowed to deteriorate as these institutions are under-funded. As a percentage of GDP, the funding of research in universities by the granting councils is less today than it was in 1970.

Under the conservative government, funding for basic research has been cut. A short-sighted government is only interested in applied research.

NRC is in a state of disrepair, lacking a president, smarting from budget cuts, stripped of the space program, waiting for the next shoe to drop. Our fledgeling industrial high technology sector is being cherry-picked by smart foreign investors while the Government of Canada stands idly by. Investment Canada has no teeth and no will to act. The Government has no vision. The established fact that foreign-owned companies tend not to do research in Canada is not even on the Government's agenda.
April 20, 1989



And small-and medium-sized businesses involved in research are harassed by accountants from Revenue Canada, a department which does not understand research.

As Denzil Doyle has pointed out, our annual trade surplus in resource-related products has only grown from about $10 billion to about $16 billion since 1976, while our annual trade deficit in medicine and high-technology products has grown from about $8 billion to about $18 billion. We had a trade deficit in computers alone of close to $5 billion last year. That means as many as 200,000 lost jobs to bright and technologically aware young Canadians.
In its recent report "R and D Outlook 1989" the Conference Board of Canada states that the general outlook for R and D spending is less positive now than it was a year ago. In considering this Bill, the question to be addressed by the House is whether the creation of this new department will assist Canada in moving forward in industrial policies and in the development of strategies for science, engineering and technology that will enable this country to create its own advantages in the global economy. I sincerely hope that the answer to that question will be in the affirmative. I hope that the move of science into a fully fledged departmental responsibility signals a greatly increased priority for it in the Government's agenda. However, the signs are that the contrary is true.
The Minister of this new Department is not a member of the Cabinet's Planning and Priorities Committee. Rather, he is one of those whose job it is to find cuts. The Government denied research, science and technology a standing committee of the House, preferring instead to structure a committee whose mandate is so broad that the concerns of the science community can only hope to be heard and addressed in a most peripheral way. There is the fear that to tie science to regional development is to link the two so that already scarce resources allocated to science are sought to be stretched even further to achieve regional development objectives.
The over-all objective of a science policy has got to be the promotion of Canada's ability to participate competitively in an international economy, increasingly driven by technological innovation. More particularly, I believe
Industrie, Science and Technology
that the objective should be to enhance the climate for technological innovation in Canada. Government should seek to stimulate and to reward innovation and should be willing to share its cost.
I believe there should be an objective of training and retraining a workforce of technologically literate workers. We require a new generation of blue and pink collar workers whose special skills will lie in the areas of working with and applying new technologies to existing jobs and in occupations that we have not even thought of yet. High tech requires trained and skilled technicians and precision machine shops. To a great extent we lack these important skills in many regions of Canada. We must have a strategy to increase in absolute and relative terms our ongoing investment in research and technological innovation. We must use our relatively small size to our advantage by encouraging co-operation between the key players. I believe the Centres of Excellence Program will contribute to this. However, that program is under-funded by the Government and has created and will continue to create tensions and rivalries in the scientific community that did not exist before.
We must improve existing incentives for the performance of industrial research. We must remove the obstacles to fair tax treatment of industrial consortia, wrestle to the ground the intractable problems of the definition of scientific research and experimental development in the Income Tax Act. We must use government procurement strategically to help create a viable advanced technology sector. We must apply strategies to accelerate commercialization of domestic and foreign technologies. Research, including applied research and international marketing, is expensive and receives direct or indirect government support in other countries. Our advanced technology must receive comparable support if it is going to gain a foothold in the global market. We should not use scarce resources to re-invent the wheel. Rather our fundamental research should be world-scale and push back the frontiers of discovery.
Fundamental research has a key role in the development of a scientific community and in setting a standard for a science culture to develop in this country. We do need to innovate, to tinker, but in our rush to be relevant, let us not abandon the pursuit of excellence in science.

April 20, 1989
Industrie, Science and Technology
Science and technology are not only crucial to our economic well-being, but could also be key to solving some of our important environmental problems. To bring the world into ecological balance will require a multiplicity of new and improved technologies. The countries that are quick to meet their own needs are also the ones whose industries are likely to grow and supply markets around the world.
In addition to a science culture in Canada, we must also beget a generation of entrepreneurs. We must recognize that entrepreneurship is a culture process and has a social value. Entrepreneurs are risk-takers. They are men and women who take a chance, and in so doing provide a pay cheque for others. They should be recognized as economic heroes.
In recent years, practically all new jobs in this country have been created in the small business sector. Working in a small business, self-employment, entrepreneurship, owning and building a company of your own, must become credible options to young people. Entrepreneurs are not bom. They are developed.

We do not intend to oppose this Bill just for the sake of opposing it, but we do intend to closely monitor all its results, Mr. Speaker.

We in the Liberal Party will support the Government if it endeavours to build the scientific base this country so desperately needs. But we will not stand idly by and be silent if the Government in its mandate continues to package its rhetoric and endeavours to sell it to us as policy. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

But rhetoric aside, I noted and listened carefully to his emphasis on the point that we must do more in Canada to train workers, whether blue or white collar workers, to put a greater emphasis on training of the workforce. I think that is something that many of us recognize as competition increases globally. Canadians have to match the skills not only of other Canadians, but workers in other countries. Given that the Hon. Member for Ottawa South has stated that point so clearly and forcefully, I just wanted to ask if he would confirm his support for the initiative announced in this House a week ago Tuesday by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) to transfer more funds and have greater emphasis on worker training under the unemployment insurance plan.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question and the opportunity it affords me to restate some of the concerns I have about the ability of Canada to provide for its scientific and technological business community the kinds of human resources that are going to be required if we are to compete in the world.
I had occasion to travel to British Columbia recently where I was able to meet with many of the advanced technology companies that are in Vancouver and Victoria. I repeatedly heard the concern expressed that the infrastructure does not exist in British Columbia to support the development of many of the companies that are there that have good products and good ideas. One critical shortage lies in the area of precision engineering machine shops. These are required if products are going to be refined and honed so that they can be tested and marketed abroad. I think that as a country we need to take a very serious look at many of educational objectives.
Many of us in this House are products of a culture that promoted the white collar above the blue. My friend who asked the question and myself are both products of legal training, and maybe that is in part a result of that. But now the time has come to stress to our young people the important jobs, the jobs of the future, are jobs that are skilled and that require scientific and technological understanding. I think that objective in our educational system is one that the federal Government needs to play a role in achieving, partly through programs that do exist but also through the support of community colleges which have been reduced in recent years. Those colleges are prime places in which to develop the kind of skilled workers that we need.
April 20, 1989

I regret the suggestion that it somehow would benefit our science community if funds were diverted from people who are unemployed in order to train people for other jobs, some of whom are already employed. I think that the need for training and skills development is clear. But where does the money come from? What I suggest to the Government is that investment in people, in science, in education should not be regarded as expenditures, but rather as investments. It will cost us much more in the long run if we do not make them than it costs in the short term to spend that money. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
