speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-3, an Act to establish the Department of Industry, Science and Technology, to repeal the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion Act and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mr. Langdon (P-724).

subtopic: INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to have the opportunity to comment on this historic legislation to create the new Department of Industry, Science and Technology.
The mandate and objectives of the new Department of Industry, Science and Technology are to strengthen the national economy, to increase international competitiveness of Canadian industry, to encourage excellence in the development and use of science and technology, and to promote economic growth and development in slow areas, areas such as Ontario and Quebec as well in outlying areas far from the central region of Ottawa.
I disagree with the amendment that was put on the floor of the House. This Government has recognized that those sitting in central Canada may not have all the tools, knowledge or facts about how to treat areas far removed, be it western Canada or Atlantic Canada, Newfoundland, northern Ontario or northern Quebec. We need to have the people in the areas who are knowledgeable and understand our differences.
During the last session of Parliament our Government created three economic development programs. One was the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency which was established in June 1987. Some $1.5 billion was transferred from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to this agency. The head office was set up in Moncton, where people from Atlantic Canada could explain their problems to people in Moncton who are knowledgeable about Atlantic Canada. In that way they could attempt to diversify and to establish agencies and companies to create jobs that are meaningful to the people who live in Atlantic Canada, rather than central Canada deciding what is good for them.
In July 1987 our Government announced the formation of FEDNOR, the northern Ontario special diversification agency. It was funded with $55 million over a five-year period from the Department of Regional and Industrial Expansion. Sault Ste. Marie has the head office, with satellite offices in Sudbury and Thunder Bay. These offices allow people to have direct input into the difficulties which people in northern Ontario face.
Northern Ontario is very different from southern Ontario, and it is the duty of the Government to recognize and understand the disparities between all regions and to use the people in the local areas to give us information.
Our Government also created the Western Diversification Fund, with its head office in your City of Edmonton, Mr. Speaker. I know you are pleased to see that we announced $1.2 billion of new funding over five years for that specific agency. This will facilitate the West in diversifying.
April 20, 1989

Industry, Science and Technology
I am very proud of the West, where we have agriculture and petroleum as our main industries. We are attempting to increase tourism, which is so important to the area.
Far too often, people in central Canada were telling people in the West what we should be doing. Westerners now have the opportunity to inform the Government and be able to have assistance in setting up new businesses. We will not compete with other companies in Canada to destroy employment levels. We want to increase our exports while cutting our imports. We are looking for new diversification, and this is what makes the Bill so interesting. This legislation strengthens science and technology but also strengthens regional development.
Prior to 1984 ERDA agreements were very popular. They were administered through the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. At that time Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia were not represented within the Liberal Government. It appeared that the funding which came to the West was extremely limited. I believe Alberta received one ERDA agreement for less than $35 million.
I am not suggesting that I am not pleased to see funding go to areas like Quebec and Ontario. It is important because we need their economic activity to balance regional disparity. I am glad that southern Ontario is active and that Quebec is improving.
However, prior to 1984 the West was simply not recognized. That is what this Government has fought for. It has listened to Members of Parliament from the outlying regions and realized that one of the biggest mistakes of the federal Government was not to listen to other knowledgeable people in the field.
We are dividing a Department to make industry, science and technology a Department that deals with the specifics of industry involvement in science and technology across Canada, while regional development is handled elsewhere.
I truly support the Government's action. I look forward to working with my Western Diversification Office, as I am sure my colleagues from the East Coast are working with their ACOA office. It is working and this is the right way to go.
We have to find ways to improve the science and technology sector, there is no doubt about that. We have learned that we cannot separate or compartmentalize various groups. We cannot have science working here,
research working over there, and industry working over there. Over the past two or three years, we have communicated with industry, with post-secondary institutions, and with junior colleges and research centres. We have worked with the various agencies and with provincial Governments.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) formed an advisory board on science and technology, bringing together 30 of the best men and women from across Canada to tell us their concerns and how we can best address them. We communicated with all these groups so that we could get the best of all worlds.
We have limited funds, and I think all Canadians recognize that now. The level of the deficit and the debt is of major importance. Of equal importance, however, is bringing together these various communities so they can zero in on how best to teach science and technology in the universities and how best to apply it to the industries so we can become more efficient, more productive and can go into the 20th century fearing no other country.
The face of international trade has changed over the last number of years. Indeed, it will change more. A great deal of our international trade was with the European community, and when the EEC was formed, we saw 12 countries come together to form an economic union. There are 350 million people involved in the EEC. It has a tremendous market-place and science and technology expertise to draw upon from various countries. It has done extremely well and has been very successful.
Canada realized that we were slowly losing our trade with western Europe. The Free Trade Agreement with the United States is one step, but we are now looking to the Pacific Rim, Japan, Korea, Indonesia and Thailand, as well as pursuing trade with our colleagues in South America. The outstanding and phenomenal Free Trade Agreement will secure our market-place with our friends south of the border, but Canadians realize that they themselves have to become more efficient. I am very pleased that we are now starting to focus on a Department that can draw the best knowledge from all areas.
I know the Hon. Member across the way mentioned that not enough has been done in areas of concern to his Party, and I agree with him. There is a lot more to be done. His concerns are also my concerns. We have started out investigating the problems, calling for all sorts of communities at all levels of education and industry to participate in finding recommendations that will solve the problems.

April 20, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
I suppose it was in the early 1980s-and you can correct me if I am wrong, Mr. Speaker, because you have been here for quite a few years longer than I have-that a program was implemented by the former Government for scientific tax credits. I believe the way that Government wanted to increase science and technology was by giving tax credits to industries that came forward with new ideas and technologies. There was an envelope of $350 million for that particular program, and in 1984 when the Conservative Government took over, it took us a year and half to resolve the difficulties with the program and less than a year to cancel it because it was being totally abused. Canadians were developing things that had already been developed or were submitting proposals that were not scientific or would not advance technology. They were simply there to grab funding.
We are dealing with taxpayers' dollars. It is the job of all Hon. Members from all sides of the House to look after the taxpayers' dollars and to see that they go into the right places, the places of need. By the time we had researched many of the proposals under that project, we found that it had cost the taxpayers $1.9 billion. Very little science and technology expertise came out of that, though perhaps a few good proposals did.
Let us put the money to good use. Let us not direct it from the Government. Let us direct it from all areas of the community so everyone can benefit and so we can get the best bang for our buck.
We must strengthen our performance in international trade. That is one of the directions being taken by this Bill. I mentioned the enhancement of the science base which will be done through the centres of excellence which were announced by the Government. We put $240 million into the centres of excellence program, an extra $200 million into the granting councils over the next few years, $80 million into Canadian Scholarship Programs as well as $500 million into technology. This indicates to me, and I think to my colleagues on this side of the House, that we do take science and technology extremely seriously.
Again, I do not suggest that this is enough, but it is a start. We have to monitor the situation constantly, and watch how well we are performing and look for ways to
make changes if so needed, or improve what we have done.
Greater attention has to be paid to developing our human resource base, and through these grants that have been made to the universities and the different agencies, we can reach out to people who are on scholarships or at universities, people who can utilize this funding. We are involving private enterprise which probably has the best knowledge of how to go about the development of science and technology.
We are creating a climate for interaction. Whether dealing with science and technology, the energy industry or the transportation industry, we have to talk to the people. That is what we have done. We talked to the people about this Bill, about the Western Accord, about the Atlantic Accord, and about the Newfoundland Accord. We are talking to the people about some tie-ups we seem to be having at Pearson International Airport, but we have resolved many of those. We are going to the people to see how they believe we should alleviate the problem.
We are not coming down from the top; we are coming up from the bottom. This is what Canadians want. We are letting them speak. We are here to represent them; we are not here to tell them how to go about their business. We are interacting and we are fostering a spirit of entrepreneurship. There is nothing greater than entrepreneurship.
Let me tell Hon. Members about a contract let by the Western Development Agency. A gentleman who lives on the outskirts of Edmonton put forward a one-page proposal to the Western Diversification Department. Fine pipe used in the petroleum industry for seismic gets all curled up and is then no good. This gentleman developed a little gadget that would straighten that pipe so it could be used over and over again. He has gotten into business and is hiring people. With this development of technology, he has created a superb business from a waste product that we had no further use for.
It is the little guys that count as well as the big guys. That is exactly what this Bill will do. It will diversify out to the regions so that we will know what the people need.
Entrepreneurship is alive and well in the West, and it is alive and well in Atlantic Canada. People in northern
April 20, 1989

Quebec have many areas of potential. Sometimes they need a little help with an extra tool or a boost with a loan or a loan guarantee. However, most of the loan guarantees through the Western Diversification Office and FEDNOR will be paid back. It might not be for five or six years. Realistically I know that not everything is 100 per cent successful, but hopefully most of them will be successful and we can almost have a self-sustaining fund where the Government has put the money into the various agencies. Western Diversification is proving this quite nicely. Over time we will be receiving money back from successful companies. Westerners do not want grants or giveaways. They just need a little boost like my colleagues in northern Quebec where there are difficulties. We are facilitating those people to become job creators. Perhaps through their own business they may create 2, 52, or 1,052 jobs. That is how we all started.
Separating regional development from science and technology and from ERDA agreements has to be the manner in which to proceed. We have put more emphasis on science and technology, and that will allow this specific Department to get right into this issue. There is no need to have Industry, Science and Technology if industries are not working with the researchers. I am very pleased to support this Bill, and I look forward to seeing it go into committee where we can have further debate.
There is no doubt that it has taken us three or four years to come up with this answer, which is the correct one for the moment. Obviously the world will change in a few years. At that point in time perhaps we will have to take another look, and perhaps it will be changed again.
The Minister has done a good job. He took DRIE and MOSST and created this new Department. The Hon. Member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) is also the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology. Under him is a specific Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Winegard), the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Hockin)-a specific Minister to keep hands on western diversification, a specific Minister to keep hands on FEDNOR, and a specific Minister to keep hands on ACOA. This means that those Ministers have a lot more direction and control over exactly what is going on.
Industry, Science and Technology
Over the last three or four years I am pleased to see that we have taken the fine words of advice from the Prime Minister's advisory council and from people across Canada. We are not telling Canadians what to do. We are working for Canadians to create a better country.

I certainly appreciate the questions of my colleague. In regard to diversifying into the outlying areas in western and Atlantic Canada, Newfoundland, northern Quebec, and northern Ontario, I do recognize that some ERDA agreements have been terminated. There is no doubt that there is still time for negotiations and time for further development in that area.
The Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), together with the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and the Prime Minister, are very concerned with the high unemployment and the situation that exists in certain regional areas of Canada. The Budget is coming down one week today. I believe that any negotiations or issuing of new ERDA agreements will be held off until after April 27. At that point in time perhaps we could address this particular question.
The Hon. Member raised the question of unemployment insurance. In her policy statement on unemployment insurance the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) did not make massive changes. We are attempting to provide funding to retrain

April 20, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
people. I take seriously the statement of the Hon. Member that there is nothing to retrain them for. I would certainly have to look into that further and more seriously.
Whether a person comes from New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, P.E.I. or Alberta, people in Canada have the spirit to get out and work. Unemployment insurance has a job to do. It has to help people who perhaps have lost their jobs. In my estimation it is not an income supplement. It is not a guaranteed income. It has to be used to retrain people. There is no sense in collecting the insurance, not taking part in retraining or returning to school, and then being faced with having to go out and seek employment when unemployment insurance terminates. I know much of the employment in the area of the Hon. Member is seasonal. I recognize that forestry and fisheries are seasonal. The area of the Hon. Member has specific problems that perhaps some areas of Canada do not have.
When a person collects unemployment insurance, he or she has to retrain. Industries are changing across Canada. What is good today may not be good tomorrow. People across Canada realize that unemployment insurance is not an income supplement or an income guarantee. It is there to help between jobs when a person is suffering. It is also there for retraining. I have to support the Minister of Employment and Immigration. She is attempting to address this issue. She has given us some excellent policy statements, and I stand behind those.
Retraining is the only manner in which the Hon. Member's constituents can get jobs. I hope to be working with people in ACOA. There is always room to improve. Nobody has the perfect solution. Perhaps we can improve ways of administering funding, or the types of industries that are being supported in order that there can be a broader base in eastern Canada.

speechtext:
I am pleased to have the opportunity to say a few words concerning regional development in the Bill which will be reorganizing the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion.
The Hon. Member for Calgary Southwest (Mrs. Sparrow) mentioned the FEDNOR program. This is a very modest program of $55 million over a five-year period for some 90 per cent of the land mass of Ontario and the whole of northern Ontario. That amount of $8 million a year in grants and some $3 million a year in loan guarantees do not go very far when we are trying to restructure industries. What we are concerned about is
whether that modest $55 million allocated for the next five-year period will survive the slaughter house that will allegedly take place a week from tonight. A report in The Toronto Star earlier this week said that deep cuts ahead are feared for the regions. It is suggested that the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion's budget will be cut from $1.3 billion to $250 million a year.
Would the Hon. Member reassure us on this side of the House that programs like FEDNOR will not be cut back? That is our first and primary concern.
The second concern relates not only to the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion but to the ERDA agreements themselves. In northern Ontario we are very dependent on the forest industry. During the last five years we have had a program for forest renewal and development in which the federal and provincial Governments each put $75 million over that five-year period. That program has run out. There has been no authorization by the Government of Canada to the officials in the Department in Sault Ste. Marie to start negotiations with the Province of Ontario. If that program is not renewed, we will see a major decline in our capacity to provide forest renewal in the years ahead. That is one ERDA agreement that has not been renewed, but there is a tourism development agreement that runs out this year as well as a native economic development agreement. If one reads the Speech from the Throne one is not sure whether any of the ERDA agreements will be renewed.
I agree that the Department is important in regional development, but ERDA agreements are important from two points of view. First, they allow the federal Government to put money into regional development programs. All the levers of economic development are not with the federal Government. Often they are in areas of provincial responsibility which allow the Government to put those funds into provincial areas. Second, it allows the Government to bring up the slow growth areas of the country to a more national average.
I would be very concerned that all we have is this Bill before us today, and we will not have ERDA agreements which allow the federal Government to put money into areas of provincial jurisdiction which are very important for economic development in a region. I hope the Hon. Member can reassure me that those funds and programs which lapsed this year will be renewed.
April 20, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. colleague for his questions. We have worked together on a few committees and I have always enjoyed our association.

FEDNOR was announced in July 1987,1 believe. This was a brand new Department which took six months to get on stream. Member's suggestions and would like to co-operate with him on how best to make FEDNOR work and work better.

subtopic: INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to Bill C-3 today, particularly to its amendments. I oppose the thrust of the Bill and the three vital flaws that I see which run counter to the stated objectives in the Bill. They are as the Bill states: to strengthen the national economy and to increase international competitiveness of Canadian industry.
By repealing the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion it is my belief the Government is signalling very clearly that it is willing to fragment the very necessary regional development tools and programs which our country has required and will continue to require to reduce the significant economic disparities present across the land. Instead of the co-ordinated program of regional development what we will end up with is a kind of hodgepodge of programs tucked away in various legislative areas with very little co-ordination or overlap.
I come from a constituency out West, Okanagan- Shuswap, in the southern interior region of British Columbia. We are still struggling, believe it or not, with unemployment levels that exceed 17 per cent. In fact, the latest figure indicates that in the northern part of my riding the unemployment level exceeds 19.6 per cent. We have real problems of regional economic disparity.
In Atlantic Canada we see that the situation is very similar to what we have out West. Both the West Coast and the East Coast remain resource driven economies that are in desperate need of economic diversification. We need a far greater commitment from the Government toward regional development than we have had in the past. We do not need the kind of legislation such as is intended in this present Bill which really serves to fragment further regional development programs and efforts.
Second, the Bill proposes that the responsibility for regional development in Ontario and Quebec shall fall under the auspices of the Ministry of Industry, Science and Technology. This implies that the economic development of the West or of Atlantic Canada with respect to science and technology will not be a primary mandate of this particular Ministry. This sends a signal to the scientific community across Canada that concentrated growth in this industry can be expected to take place in Central Canada. Once again, we see evidence that the Government is intending to provide favouritism to Central Canada at the expense of its regions, such as the West and Atlantic Canada. It makes me wonder whether the Government has ever realized that there is life west of the Rocky Mountains.

April 20, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
There is a good deal of scientific research going on out West and a good deal of potential for increased research efforts. As has been the case for so long, the attention has been centred in mainly two provinces, Ontario and Quebec. We are losing scientific talent from the West, simply because of a chronic lack of research and development capital. We are losing prime opportunities for economic diversification and technological advancement in our western provinces because of this Government's centralist attitude toward economic development and reducing regional disparities.
I trained as a biochemist. I worked for some time in the research community in British Columbia. I noticed first-hand a chronic lack of research funding, not totally the fault of this Government. Much of the blame has to placed upon the shoulders of the provincial Government. Certainly, there has been a chronic lack of funding by both institutions with regard to research and development.

This fact is widely recognized to the point that the Prime Minister pledged to double Canada's spending on research and development during his Governments first term of office.

this industry in Canada today. It fails to recognize the commitment that this Government made back in the election campaign. speechtext:
My colleague says: " Some day". We on this side are still waiting for that day.
There was a most illuminating comment made on October 23, 1986, by my colleague, the Member for Beausejour, (Mr. Robichaud), in his comments, in the Commons debates. I would like to read these comments into the record. Mr. Robichaud stated: "The Government has bragged about having created an independent portfolio for tourism". What happened to the Department of Tourism in the Cabinet's last shuffle? In June last, the Prime Minister simply struck it off. The Department of Tourism is no more. We now have a Minister of State for Small Business and Tourism (Mr. Hockin). TIAC chairman, Walter Tilden, expressed his disappointment by stating that: "It would appear that the Government does not know what to do with tourism. The executive director of the Tourism Industry Association of Canada, John Lawson, also expressed disappointment by stating:
"We are back to a combined Ministry. It is a clear sign that tourism is once again relegated to a backroom". Those comments were made on October 23, 1986. Unfortunately, I would like to submit to you that things have not changed. The Government is once again relegating tourism to the backroom of economic development. The Hon. Minister of State is probably reluctant to make an issue out of this. I do not blame him. One does not want to bite the hand that feeds you. I would like to help out my colleague, the Hon. Minister, in our mutual attempts to increase the economic clout of his
Industry, Science and Technology
Department. It is easier for me to criticize the Government, than it is for him to do so.
Canada's tourism industry has a bigger international market than lumber, newsprint, or crude petroleum, and it outperforms wheat and natural gas combined. We are not talking about a small economic impact. It has a growth rate which, for the past 10 years, surpassed that of the major industrial sectors. It pumps $21 billion into the national economy, $6.3 billion of which is foreign revenue. Nationally, the industry employs 600,000 people directly, and another 500,000 indirectly. Over 600,000 tourism businesses are in Canada, the majority of which are small and mid-size operations, where 80 per cent of our job creation takes place. Tourism revenue pumps $9 billion annually into government coffers. Some 6.7 cents of every dollar spent in Canada is spent on its tourism products. Through this legislation the Government wants to delegate the Department of Tourism to the back-burner of economic development by hiding it within the proposed Ministry of Industry, Science and Technology.
Tourism is Canada's fastest growing industry. Throughout every province it has ranked first in the creation of new jobs. There is no other industry which has contributed more to Canada's regional development. I do not think that the Government will give my colleague, the Minister of State for Tourism (Mr. Hockin), the opportunity to oversee a Ministry of full status.
Tourism is already the largest industry in Canada. From 1975 to 1985 the workforce in tourism-related industries has in fact grown by some 90 per cent. By the year 2000 it is expected that it will be the leading industry in Canada. I wish to read to Hon. Members a statement from a 1988 Tourism Canada publication entitled The Challenge in Tourism Product Development. This is from a Ministry circular. It states: "Given the growth potential and the significant economic contribution in Canada the key question is whether or not Canada can in fact meet the expectations of the market-place in the future, particularly with respect to the quality of its tourism product which will play a large part in determining the future success of the tourism industry". The key comment that this publication makes is with respect to whether or not we can meet the expectations of the market-place and that in Canada it is critical that we become globally competitive in the tourism industry.

April 20, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
Although tourism is a growth industry, our international tourism deficit has increased over the last few years. It is also steadily growing. We have reached an all-time high in our tourism trade deficit. We now have a deficit that is at $5.2 billion annually. That figure is taken directly from this Ministry circular.
I submit that to remain globally competitive in the international tourism market-place we will have to do better than we have in developing and marketing our tourism product. It will take initiatives that can only be developed if we have a full-fledged tourism Ministry, not a miniscule Department that is buried in the confines and the bowels of some other Ministry.
The Tourism Industry Association of Canada has repeatedly called for the establishment of a separate Ministry of Tourism with an equal status to other major economic sectors. Over the last 10 years the federal investment in tourism marketing has not even kept pace with inflation. We have now reached the point at which some individual states in the United States of America spend more on tourism marketing and tourism development than does the Government of Canada. I suggest that our efforts have to be doubled and redoubled. It is not enough for an industry that is poised throughout the world to become the largest world-wide by the 21st century. I think we will have to do a lot more in order to catch up to this very rapidly changing global market in tourism.
The tourism industry is not satisfied with anything less than a full-fledged Ministry of Tourism. The Government made a public commitment eight years ago to highlight tourism and to give it the promotion that it deserves today. This Bill clearly demonstrates that the promise has been broken and that tourism will continue to be treated as a junior Department with a budget that is inadequate to do the job.
In summary, once again the Government is demonstrating its modus operandi of the last few years of not spoiling a good election promise by actually doing something about it. I would like to recommend that the Government consider the striking of the Department of Tourism as an adjunct to the Ministry of Industry, Science and Technology, as is recommended in this legislation.
Finally, I would like also to recommend that the Government introduce further legislation that would in fact establish a separate and full-fledged Ministry of Tourism. I would add that we have to provide the legislative clout to ensure that the tourism industry receive the kind of attention and the kind of federal commitment that it deserves today.

subtopic: INDUSTRY, SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during its first mandate, the Government had an opportunity to thoroughly examine each and every area of activities, each and every industry. Our goal was to take stock of the situation as it existed in Canada and determine our strong and weak points in order to develop strategies to successfully meet the challenges of our world and those of future generations.
As each Member of this House could realize, the Government has done away with the practice of developing policies in isolation, because, in this respect, past federal Governments have had a very poor record. Since 1984, this Government has defined itself as one of openness and consultation. That is why we have set up consultation mechanisms wherever the efficient intervention of the State was required.
April 20, 1989

Mr. Speaker, the tourist industry was certainly no exception. During our research and consultations, we have come up with extremely eloquent data. For instance, in Canada, no industry creates as many jobs as tourism. Some 600,000 Canadians earn their living in that industry and hold a great many types of occupations.
Mr. Speaker, 600,000 people are working in the tourist industry. That represents approximately 5 per cent of the jobs nationwide. In terms of revenues, I have checked the lastest available statistics, those of 1987, and I have found that foreign tourists had spent nearly $21 billion in Canada.
I will go further and say that the tourist industry creates more jobs than the airspace, financial services and agricultural industries. I would go even further. Tourist-related activities rank second, right behind the automobile industry in terms of total production and job creation.
Finally, the tourist industry outmatches the car industry in terms of economic growth as well as job creation. Tourism certainly deserves our full attention, for it is much more than just a pleasant distraction. We must see it as a dynamic economic force in full expansion.
As a consequence, the Government had no choice but to take action and make sure that the tourist industry maintains and even accelerates its growth. As I was saying a while ago, our initial approach to this issue was based on consultation with the main players in every region of this great country.
For example, our Government has organized the national convention on the tourism of tomorrow, which brought together the private sector and all levels of government to review their respective priorities and strengthen their co-operation.
We have also established the tourism ministers conference and the Tourism Marketing Council, among other things.
The Canadian Government has sponsored the most ambitious study ever done on the American pleasure travel market. We were more than willing to share the findings of that research with the provinces and the private sector. As far as tourism is concerned, the Government is convinced that any action to strengthen an industry must be taken in a true spirit of solidarity.
Industry, Science and Technology
As I was saying, tourism is one of Canada's most important economic activities in terms of sales, revenue in strong foreign currency, tax revenue and job creation. Are we to believe that the growth rate of our international tourism will keep on climbing? Among factors conducive to tourism, the sustainable economic prosperity of industrialized countries comes in first place.
Until now, it is the industrialized western countries which have done the most for tourism development. But the Communist countries are now experiencing a remarkable economic expansion. No wonder many analysts predict that by the year 2000 tourism will be the biggest industry in the world.
Canada's performance since 1980, Mr. Speaker, is quite impressive, especially in comparison with our main competitors. Those are not my words but those of the World Tourism Organization, which reports every year in American dollars the international revenue of major countries, excepting the transportation cost of international travellers.
Indeed, from 1980 to 1987, Canada's international tourism revenue increased by 8.2 per cent annually on average, compared to 6.2 per cent for the United States and 5.2 per cent for the United Kingdom, for example. In fact, our country is ninth in the world for international tourism revenue.
I do not think it is an exaggeration, Mr. Speaker, to predict that Canada made the right choice in time and that its future prospects are excellent. But there is no question of stopping along the way and presuming arbitrarily that the game is already won. We have realized that as the number of travelers increases, so does the competition.
We must also recognize that tourists are more and more demanding. If we do not act to meet their expectations, we will have to forget about the exciting prospects the future holds in store for us.
Obviously, it is in our country's interest to have a well-articulated tourism development strategy that leaves nothing to chance. For this, Mr. Speaker, we need to know our major tourist attractions perfectly and do everything to market them.
So what are these combinations of attractions, events and services that have come to be called "tourism products"? You will see that we are very well endowed in this regard. Canada can pride itself in four major tourism products which have proven themselves over the years. First comes our outstanding strong point, traveling tourism.

April 20, 1989
Industry, Science and Technology
Certainly, the diversity of our scenery, our wild coastline and millions of acres of almost undisturbed nature put us in a class by ourselves.
Mr. Speaker, keep in mind that Canada has a network of 34 national parks and wildlife reserves. These parks would play a larger role still if they had improved animation services and close at hand top-quality lodging facilities, and if they were open for a longer period.
No-one maintains that Canada's climate is ideal for year-round tourism, but that is no reason to go into hibernation the moment the first snow flake hits the ground. On the contrary, we ought to take the initiative and make the best we can with the kind of activities which are appropriate on colder days.
Mr. Speaker, this bring me to our second, most sought-after product: open air tourism, sports, and adventure. We are highly competitive in that sector, what with land and water excursions, hunting and fishing, safaris and other activities which attract higher income travelers.
The third element of potential growth has to be urban tourism. In recent years our infrastructures in urban centres has undergone tremendous development. Such industrial and cultural centres as Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver and Ottawa offer top-notch attractions in gastronomy, entertainment, quality accomodation, and shopping opportunities, to name a few. Urban tourism is growing, and although some progress has been made our major cities still have a long way to go to project a stronger image and appeal.
Mr. Speaker, this gives you an idea of the state of tourism in Canada, and it could be the starting point of the Government's strategy.
As I pointed out earlier, Mr. Speaker, Canada's advantages are well known the world over. I might add that our country's excellent reputation as a pacific and welcoming nation can only serve the interests of the tourist industry.
Canada can rightfully be looked upon as a haven of peace, and our hospitable climate is attracting international tourist. Still, Mr. Speaker, competition is becoming stiffer because, not unlike Canada, the goverment of all industrialized countries strongly support tourism and spare no effort to lure the traveling public who is increasingly being sought after worldwide.
Our research indicate that the number of tourists who might visit Canada is likely to increase significantly over the next six years. We estimate that if we make a concerted marketing effort and accurately pinpoint the winning destinations we might be able to double our income from international tourism by 1994 and reach $14 billion.
Among other things, our free trade agreement with the United States will make it easier for Canadians and Americans to visit one another. That is a factor which ideally underlies our strategic approach to tourism, for obviously the United States is our best costumer.
We intend to intensify our efforts in areas of highest growth potential, namely the South Atlantic States, those among the Central Atlantic Coast, New England and the Rockies.
In addition to the expected flow of neighbours from down South, we have noted a seemingly irreversible movement of Asian tourists to whom Canada's natural beauty is a tremendous fascination.
In that respect an estimated 10 million Japanese tourists could cross over next year, almost double the number in 1985. To Canada this is a potential market we have no intention of neglecting, Mr. Speaker, especially since the Japanese of all international tourists are the ones with the highest per capita expenditurrate.
Far from us to neglect more traditional European markets. More French visitors come here each year, just as West German and British ones. Those are nations higly sought after by every country having even a small degree of sophistication in their tourist infrastructures. We not are the only ones in the race, Mr. Speaker, but if Canada can intensify its development and marketting efforts abroad, we will increase in proportion our share of the international market. Like my colleague Tom Hockin, the Minister of State (Small Business and Tourism), I think we will have to predict future trends and thereby get ahead of the competition.
Being a with a country relatively small population and rather modest promotion and advertising financial resources for that reason, we will have to be innovative and creative if we are to catch the imagination of potential tourists. There again the collegial approach, the sharing of our talents and initiatives will play a capital role.
April 20, 1989

We also identified the nature of the basic problems we must tackle to improve our tourist industry's performance. Those problems arise mainly in the areas of finance, human resources and technological adjustment.
Concerning finance, the Government is committed to gradually eliminating the imbalances that historically restricted small entrepreneurs from accessing major sources of financing. The new order that is being established in the tax regime, combined with financial circles increased awareness of the tourist industry's spinoffs, certainly will help support the initiatives of those who believe in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the quality of service, a matter directly linked to the scarecity of skilled human resources, also is a major concern.
In fact, fewer young people are available, and fewer are interested in a career in the restaurant and hotel industry, for instance. However, we cannot provide first class service without professional, well-trained staff.
We all have a responsibility to make the tourism industry more attractive to Canadian workers. We need innovative ideas and effective marketing programs to reverse a trend that is worrisome, to say the least. The Government has guaranteed its unconditional support for all types of employers who for a long time have been anxious to improve the quality of service in the tourism industry.
As for adjusting to new technologies, Mr. Speaker, our hotel chains, airline companies and travel wholesalers made that adjustment a number of years ago. Our transportation, accommodation, guided tours, entertainment and restaurants are first class, except for a certain lack of co-ordination between these sectors. We have the tools to take care of the necessary planning, but there is a certain form of misplaced individualism that seems to undermine this kind of co-ordination. We hope that our appeal for better co-operation will be answered, Mr. Speaker.
If we are prepared to tackle the problem head on and organize more package tours, Canada's reputation as a host of international calibre will continue to improve.
Industry, Science and Technology
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to summarize the pros and cons of tourism in Canada. I have made an attempt to zero in on our priorities and determine what obstacles had to be overcome. I would now like to comment briefly on the fundamental goals of the federal Government's tourism development strategy. ABORIGINAL PEOPLES-SUSPENSION OF HUNGER   STRIKE-MINISTER'S UNDERTAKING-REQUEST FOR COMMITMENT ON FUNDING-NEGOTIATIONS WITH ELECTED NATIVE LEADERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I first rose in this House to question the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) over changes to native education policy two weeks ago, I was optimistic. I believed that the Minister was a reasonable person and in the interest of resolving the dispute he could agree to two simple things. First, there must be negotiations with the people affected by the policy. Second, the changes should not be implemented while negotiations are taking place. This seemed reasonable to me.
This Government claims to be willing to discuss its policies with anyone affected by them. Surely the same courtesy should be extended to native people as well. After all, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has entertained a steady parade of business groups and Conservative think-tanks during the preparation of his Budget. In fact, the Hon. Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) recently defended meetings with the infamous Fraser Institute in the name of open consultation.
It seemed reasonable that the new policy dealing with Indian post-secondary education would be put on hold while the negotiations took place. If fair and open negotiations are to take place it seems that both sides must be willing to change their position and not come to the table with preconceived ideas, otherwise no true negotiation can take place.
Last week, I rose again to question the Minister on this matter. My optimism was dimmed somewhat but I still believed that the Minister was open to reason. I asked him to reconsider his refusal to begin negotiations, emphasizing the increasing danger to the health of the fasting Indian students. Incredibly, it is necessary to continue this debate. As we all know, there will be a debate on the subject over the next two days.
In good faith most of the fasting students called off their fast last weekend. In return, they expected the Minister to keep his promise to begin bilateral negotiations.
In this spirit of renewal they met with the Minister on Tuesday, along with representatives of Indian leadership. However, the Minister betrayed this spirit of renewal. He stated at that meeting that he would not impose a

April 20, 1989
Adjournment Debate
moratorium. On the one hand the Minister insists on good faith, his willingness to compromise and his openness to new ideas. Yet, on the other hand, he presents native people with a fait accompli. How can Indian people engage in meaningful negotiations if the policy is all ready to be implemented and already decided upon? By making up his mind before hearing the analysis offered by First Nations from across the country the Minister is not negotiating in good faith in this issue.
Earlier, the Minister refused to negotiate when the students were fasting, saying he would not be held hostage. Yet at the same time he wants to hold the negotiating process hostage to his own artificial deadlines. He makes up his mind and then asks for native contributions. The Minister has made a mockery of the consultative process that the Government represents as part of its strategy.
In response to the Minister's stubborn refusal to negotiate in good faith, several students have continued their fast. Melinda and Debbie Sault are on their twenty-ninth day of a hunger-strike. I spoke to their mother just a few days ago. I have spoken to other hunger-strikers in Saskatoon also. They are concerned with their weight loss. They are concerned with their health. They are concerned, as doctors are, that permanent damage to their health could occur as their bodies start digesting themselves.
This has been a life and death situation and remains one for these young people. Yet the Minister has turned a deaf ear to their plea. All they want is to negotiate and to delay implementation until negotiations are complete. Is this unreasonable? I think it is not. I do not think any person giving it a moment's thought would think it an unreasonable request. Yet the Minister has continued to deny them.
The support for Indian post-secondaiy education is a moral and historical obligation of the Canadian Government. Our country is built on an enormously valuable land-base provided by our First Nations. In return, natives were promised many things, including education. This year, 15,000 students attended post-secondary institutions. Yet native participation in post-secondary education in Canada is still far below the rate for non-Indian students. The program has grown over the past 10 years. Many students have graduated. Some 90 per cent of those graduates find jobs. Education is the key to native future, to the future of our first peoples. Yet the Government wants to cut off this future.
The decision of the Minister and the previous Minister to cap funding for native post-secondary education is both unjust and immoral. However, given that morality and justice are foreign to this Government, let me turn to an argument based on economics to which it seems to be much more in tune.
In the name of financial efficiency the Post-secondary Assistance Program has been kept. No longer will funds be provided to meet demand but individual bands will be required to allocate funds only to some students. Rationing of education will take place. The bands will be divided. The budget is limited, and that ends the thinking process of this Government.
If this is false economy, what is more expensive, four years of education or 40 years of welfare? Native people are mired in poverty and unemployment. Education is a proven way out. Educating native people today will save millions in welfare, penitentiary and health expenditures tomorrow. Where is the good business sense this Government claims to have? Where is the compassion the Government claims to have?

Mr. Speaker, on April 7, 1989, the Hon. Member for Saskatoon- Clark's Crossing (Mr. Axworthy) raised concerns about the bilateral process for reviewing Indian post-secondary policy. I would like to provide some background to this matter so that there might be a better understanding of the commitment by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) to a joint review of the policies with the Indian leaders, students and Department officials.
The new policy has major improvements over the previous program. These have resulted from consultation with over 500 Indian bands, with tribal councils, with students and educators. These are consultations which took place in 1988.
The program provides tuition assistance. It provides a new approach to the provision of living allowances. It provides adjustments to the rates of assistance, including special allowances for high rental areas. In addition, up to 5 per cent of the students will be eligible for scholarships of $3,500 for successful study in a range of programs supporting self-government and economic development. Also, the new policy includes an annual scholarship of up to $1,000 based on academic achievement.
April 20, 1989

The Government is committed to Indian post-secondary education. In the Minister's letter to the chiefs and councils on March 20, 1989, he indicated that the budget for the program rose from $4.2 million in 1975-76 to over $130 million in 1989-90. It is the Government's intention to continue to meet any future increased demand for post-secondary assistance through controlled budgetary increases.
The objective of the new policy, which is to apply to students enrolling this September, 1989, is to produce more graduates, and to encourage students to take programs of study which would assist Indian self-government and economic self-reliance.
The previous policy was deemed inadequate by the Assembly of First Nations in its review of education. Now, as a result of the new policy, Indian education authorities have increased control over their own administration of student assistance programs.
The Minister has indicated on many occasions that once the hunger-strike is over he is ready to undertake a bilateral process of discussion over the next few months to review the policy, to try to resolve any outstanding concerns and issues. These discussions would involve both the students and the Indian leaders. The Government is looking forward to a continuation of this very successful program.

Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to participate in the adjournment debate this evening. However, before I do, I want to make a couple of brief comments unrelated to the subject matter at hand.
First, if I could be a bit of a John Warren, I would like to let people know that immediately after the adjournment the Newfoundland election will be carried on the parliamentary channel, followed by the rerun of Question Period today. I say that just in case anybody is out there watching.
Second, I want to congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Belsher), on his appointment as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport. The Hon. Member was involved considerably in the Transport Committee in the previous Parlia-
Adjournment Debate
ment. I know that he will bring to his new position an understanding of the issues as well as with respect to how the Transport Committee works. I look forward to working with him.
I did something that I don't like to do, Mr. Speaker, and it is something that I haven't done in a previous Parliament. I requested that a Minister of the Crown be removed from office. I did it after great thought. I did it not because somebody else had already suggested the same thing time and time again. Too often in this House the immediate reaction is that if we don't like something that has happened, it is off with the head of the Minister.
I think what has been happening in Transport over the last five years is a lack of control. It has been getting worse. In our parliamentary system, it is the Minister who is ultimately responsible for what happens. Now the current Minister is a gentleman. I have no hesitation whatsoever in saying that. He is stuck with a real problem.
It started with the Deputy Prime Minister, then Minister of Transport, who followed the lead of the Liberals in deregulating air transportation and other modes. The Minister for International Trade did not appear to care about what was happening within the Ministry. Now a Minister has inherited a Ministry that is driving the ship. In a lot of ways, it is providing him with advice that is less than appropriate for what has happened in the industry.
Why do I say all this? When we were dealing with the White Paper Freedom To Move, when we were dealing with Bills C-18 and C-19, there were two favourite expressions. The Government, Minister after Minister, said that this new policy of leaving it to the market-place as opposed to public convenience and necessity would in no way endanger safety, that safety was the number one concern of the Government. In no way would they allow any of this to have a negative impact.
The Liberal Party, in their re-found, rebom-again opposition to deregulation-they were the ones who started it in Canada. There is no question about that. The Member for, I believe, Fort Garry was the one who, as Transport Minister initiated it. We were saying, "Listen, there are going to be some problems created. When it comes down to a decision between meeting the

April 20, 1989
Adjournment Debate
bankers' demands and being concerned about safety, even though you don't like to do it, and we were thinking of the small carriers on the air side, one would end up having to meet the bankers' demand of payment versus that extra $500 cost for de-icing a plane or replacing a wheel-bearing." Even though the specs said it was good for another 200 miles, the industry norm was replacing it then. It was held off. We suggested that those kinds of things were going to happen. We were pooh-poohed. We were told at the time that that is not going to happen. These companies are responsible. They would never jeopardize safety.
As we have seen in the United States where equipment is being used for longer and longer periods of time, we have major structural failures. We have one airplane that looks more like a convertible, another that loses a door, others that have cracked wings. All of these planes are in the 20-year age group ,which under a regulated environment in the United States, because of the stability of the industry, and stability means a decent bottom line, means that those planes would have been replaced at an appropriate time.
Instead, because of the nature of the competition, drastic reduction in fares in some cases, and we have seen in the States the number of airlines going out of business, that kind of competition has pushed the carriers to the limit. They have used their equipment longer than they should have. We are seeing the results of that.
In Canada, while we in the Opposition were being pooh-poohed when we warned that this could potentially lead to accidents or failures of equipment, deaths or injury, Transport Canada was saying to the Deputy Minister of Transport that resources were not available to deal properly with the deregulation of air in Canada. It said:
The shortage of trained, experienced inspection staff and other personnel has seriously impacted on the Directorate's ability to effectively perform its mandated tasks. The increase in the certification workload under economic regulatory reform, resulting from the need to service new and expanding air carriers, is affecting the Directorate's ability to effectively complete its ongoing inspection program, and thereby assure industry compliance with established legislation, regulation and standards.
It goes on and on. This is an internal audit branch document, a preliminary review of aviation regulations given to the Deputy Minister of Transport in June, 1987, the very same month that this House passed Bills C-18 and C-19.
It was October of that year when the first part of those Bills was proclaimed. This Government knew, at least at the bureaucratic level. I cannot believe the Deputy Minister did not advise the Minister at the time that this document existed and of the warnings that were out there. Yet the Government did nothing about this. It did not make sure there were air traffic controllers. It did not make sure there were inspectors, et cetera.
I look forward, Mr. Speaker, to the response from the Parliamentary Secretary. He knows, I know and you know that we are going to continue this battle another time as we put in place the preventive measures necessary.

Mr. Speaker, it would appear that the Government has in fact reached a final decision as to its response to the GATT ruling of 1987 which found against the current regulations which have prevented the export of raw, pink and sockeye salmon and of herring from British Columbia. However, a number of issues remain. For example, in the new regulations which we are told are to be issued, there is the question of which specific provisions they will contain in terms of grading and inspection of the fish landed.
The concern has been raised that all that will occur is that raw fish will be landed at landing stations in British Columbia only to be purchased by American buyers and shipped directly to the United States.
The Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), has given the House his assurance that the so-called "Murphy 2" proposal will be rejected by Canada. This proposal would have permitted Canadian fish caught by Canadian vessels to be shipped directly to U.S. ports where a Canadian official would be able to count the fish for the purpose of our conservation efforts. For Canada to even entertain such a proposal is totally unacceptable to British Columbia's fishermen and to the industry.
Adjournment Debate
On another point, what effect have the efforts of the U.S. Trade Representative, Carla Hills, had on influencing the Canadian Government? According to a statement from the U.S. Trade Representative's office on March 28, hearings will be conducted into which Canadian fish products will be targeted for further trade sanction actions.
The list which was released by the U.S. trade office lists 18 fish products. I will just mention those that are appropriate to the B.C. coast. They include salmon, whether it be canned, filletted, smoked or salted; turbot, filletted; other fish roe; other fish, filletted; other fish, minced or not. It would seem to include almost every commercial product processed in British Columbia.
In the communique issued by the Trade Representative's office, the public, particularly the U.S. industry, is being invited to propose additions to the list just in case anything was left out.
If the Government accepts the provision whereby fish would be landed in Canada without any processing whatsoever, only to be sold in the U.S. in the hope of avoiding U.S. trade action, I believe it is being extremely naive.
Section 304(e) of the American implementing legislation of the Free Trade Agreement states the following:
(1)	Within 30 days of the application by Canada of export controls on unprocessed fish under statutes exempted from the Agreement under Article 1203, or the application of landing requirements for fish caught in Canadian waters, the President shall take appropriate action to enforce United States rights under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade that are retained in Article 1205 of the Agreement.
(2)	In enforcing the United States rights referred to in paragraph (1), the President has discretion to-
(A)	bring a challenge to the offending Canadian practices before
the GATT;
(B)	retaliate against such offending practices;
(C)	seek resolution directly with Canada;
(D)	refer the matter for dispute resolution to the Canada-United
States Trade Commission; or
(E)	take other action that the President considers appropriate to
enforce such United States rights.
Thus, within a month of any new landing requirements, regardless of how ineffective they might be, the Americans are more than likely to begin the process of trade action against them.
Fishermen, as represented by their unions, and our fishing industry have joined in expressing concern that Canada may give in to the United States pressure with respect to the West Coast industry. The fear is that our Government may do this in the hope that the United States will not take any similar steps with regard to the East Coast.

April 20, 1989
Adjournment Debate
If they win, the next time the Americans could demand that East Coast restrictions be brought into line with the GATT. Article 1205 of the trade agreement states: "The parties retain their rights and obligations under GATT and agreements negotiated under GATT". Thus the exempted provincial provisions could be open for challenge before GATT.
Given the precedent of giving in on the sea regulations, they are more likely than ever to fall by the wayside as well.
As Geoff Meggs, editor of The Fisherman in British Columbia, said: "If we have lost our right to process our own fish then how can we require that Canadians catch the fish in the first place?"
On March 21, 1988, the former Minister for International Trade told the House that salmon and herring caught off the Pacific Coast will be landed in Canada in order to ensure accurate catch reporting, inspection, grading and quality control. Will the Government today declare forthrightly and unequivocally that it intends to live up to those words?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member opposite knows that this complaint which originated with the U.S. fishing interests in Alaska, was that Canadian processors were buying up substantial quantities of Alaskan salmon and herring while U.S. processors were denied any access to unprocessed salmon and herring from Canada. The U.S. took the issue to the GATT where a clear finding was made that the Canadian export restrictions on unprocessed Pacific pink and sockeye salmon and herring violated international trade rules.
In March, 1988, the Government announced that it would remove the GATT inconsistent export restrictions. The Government's announcement also stated that concurrent with this removal, new GATT-consistent regulations would be introduced to ensure that salmon and herring caught off the Pacific Coast will continue to be landed in Canada, to ensure that our well recognized fish conservation and management programs are not compromised.
The Government undertook an extensive consultative process in 1988, to seek industry's views respecting the development of a GATT-consistent landing requirement which would ensure maintenance of the conservation and management system related to Pacific salmon and herring. An industry advisory committee was created which, in September, 1988, submitted a series of recommendations for consideration.
The recommendations were subjected to an extensive review and analysis, including an evaluation by eminent independent GATT experts, to ascertain if the proposed landing requirement system would be GATT-consistent. The answer was yes, and the system, developed with the industry and the independent GATT experts, was discussed with the United States and is now part of the regulatory amendments.
Throughout this issue the Government has maintained the position that Canada will fulfil its GATT obligations while at the same time safeguarding the essential interests of the West Coast fishing industry through GATT-consistent regulations.
The regulatory package requiring the landing of both Pacific salmon and herring at shore based landing stations has been fully reviewed and supported by the industry and the Province of British Columbia. The Government has been moving on a fast track to implement the new regulations and it is expected that they will be completed before April 26, 1989.
With respect to the Pacific herring roe extraction activity, the Government is determined to ensure that this activity will continue to be carried out in Canada through measures that are GATT-consistent. Various possible measures are under consideration in consultation with the industry.
